speechtext:
The House resumed from Wednesday, May 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Hockin that Bill C-126, an Act to amend the Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee, and the amendment of Mr. Skelly:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"Bill C-126, An Act to amend the Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act, be not now read a second time but that it be read a second time this day six months hence."

subtopic: BRETTON WOODS AND RELATED AGREEMENTS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Bill before us today, Bill C-126, is an Act to amend the Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act. It provides for two amounts, one of $550 million and one of $250 million. The terms of the loans are favourable but will be used mainly to service existing debts. Third World debt, as many Canadians know, is over $1 trillion and rising. In 1987 Third World countries paid the IMF $5.9 billion more than they received and commercial banks now take more than they lend, a situation that has been going on for some time. Development assistance is drying up and, despite what our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) promised, which was to reach .7 per cent of our Gross National Product by 1990, that goal was moved to 1995 and has now been moved on into the 21st century, a promise which the Government of Canada should clearly have met. Stephen Lewis, our Ambassador to the United Nations, said in an interview with the Vancouver Sun on May 9:
The West is betraying the African continent.
The debts of sub-Sahara and African countries are not as large in absolute numbers as those of, say, Brazil or Mexico, but when expressed as a percentage of their Gross National Product or their debt service to export ratio, the debts are devastating. The IMF imposes structural reforms on these nations, and as one official put it, "cheaper money for stricter policies". These social costs of adjustment are borne most heavily by the very poor. The policies that were passed by my Party at its most recent convention deal directly with the social problems that were created by the coercion of the IMF and of developed nations on Third World nations. Our Convention Policy, B.3.2, reads in part:
... The IMF, in pursuit of monetarist objectives has imposed conditions upon Third World countries which have led to drastic devaluation of currencies, reduction of already low wage levels, elimination of food subsidies and cut-backs in social services. Enforcement of these unpopular policies has required repressive internal security measures which are directly counter to development...
It goes on to call upon the Canadian Government to respond positively to Third World proposals for immediate debt relief such as the repayment of a rate equal to a ceiling of 10 per cent of export earnings proposed by Peruvian President, Alan Garcia.
Specifically, we oppose tying a debt to domestic export development. What developing countries need most is a commitment from countries like Canada to long-term infrastructural development assistance of the kind that will allow a broad based and self-sustainable economic and social development in the recipient countries. That was put on the record some time ago, in fact on September 10 of last year, by our House Leader from Kamloops

Shuswap.
The IMF is not a neutral economic instrument, benevolently assisting Third World nations in a disinterested fashion. Voting on the IMF executive board is weighted by size of contribution, meaning that the United States has a predominant influence, and hence the emphasis on structural reform meaning a tax on social programs, on local self-development and so on. This Government has not opposed the use of the international banking system for right wing purposes, as we saw with the refusal of loans to Nicaragua.
It is time to develop a new system of international credit. The Bretton Woods agreement no longer works. It was developed in 1944 under very different economic conditions. The United States was the mainstay of that system. It had a commitment to multilateralism and the U.S. dollar was the

unassailable basis of world currency. However, the U.S. no longer operates on a truly multilateral basis. Instead, multilateral institutions are seen under the Reagan administration as an extension of domestic policy. The U.S. dollar no longer serves to stabilize and facilitate the world economy. The current function of the market system serves to drive down world commodity prices, worsening Third World Governments' balance of payment problems.
An example is one of the areas hardest hit, as pointed out by Stephen Lewis, and that is the sub-Sahara of Africa and certainly the whole of the continent of Africa. We have seen a fall in commodity prices there. They fell from a base of 100 in 1980 to 61.1 by 1986, and the fall continues. The solution of export-driven development simply serves to increase problems.
The Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly), who has done a great deal of work in relation to CIDA and Third World problems for our Party, has said:
When prices drop for Third World countries they often respond by
producing more. Our whole economic system is based on the fact that in order
to compete people have to produce more.
When everybody produces more it creates a glut on the market and, as a
result, commodity prices fall further.
The Bill before us today, Bill C-126, provides funds in two different ways to a particular section of the IMF with which I will deal in a moment. Canada's record is not good in this area. As I said, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has not been able to get the assistance of his Cabinet colleagues on the Treasury Board to move forward with a more substantive role in dealing with the debts of the Third World. While our record in that area is not good, it is still better than that of most industrialized countries. There is clearly a need for a new international economic order, and I am saddened that this Government and this country have not taken more seriously, either in terms of within Canada-

Thank you, Madam Speaker. That was very helpful.
Many Canadians were hoping that the Government would take more seriously the recommendations of the World Commission on the Environment chaired by Prime Minister Brundtland which brought forward in a very real way the problems of the globe as a whole and why we need to move more vigorously toward the concept of sustainable development, not only within Canada but around the world. One of the problems faced on the African continent and in other Third World countries is the fact that the nature of the IMF loan process does not allow for or promote the concept of sustainable development.
Bill C-126 provides a loan base up to $550 million to the Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility, known as the
ESAF, of the International Monetary Fund. ESAF was initiated at the 1987 Venice Summit of the G-7. It called for an increase to $10 billion, more than double the amount that was sought in 1986.
Second, Bill C-126 provides for a grant of up to $250 million to the same body. The $550 million in the first part of the Bill is a loan that can be made through the ESAF at market interest rates and then the money is loaned by the IMF on concessional terms. This money is for the highly indebted and poor countries, largely in the south Sahara of Africa. The money is used to support structural adjustment programs aimed at restoring the balance of payments and promoting economic growth.
It is good to provide help, but often the structural adjustment programs are too stringent or promote developments that are overly export oriented and not sustainable and provide little if any real benefit to local populations. As we have noted in many countries around the world, the local populations in fact have to give up wages, housing conditions and even food in order to meet the structural adjustment programs imposed upon them by the IMF.
Canada's expense in relation to the Bill is the difference between the loan rates of, say, .5 per cent in terms of the loan to a Third World country and what would have been received commercially, and that will work out to about $30 million per year to be added to our $2.7 billion foreign aid programs.
I would like to spend a moment dealing with what some of those so-called foreign aid programs are. They are often raised by my constituents, and I know in the past, they have been raised by Members of the House. Canadians generally support very strongly the provision of assistance, whether through funds like the one before us today or through our foreign aid programs.
On November 10, 1987, I received a letter from the Secretary of State for External Affairs, which reads:
Dear Jim:
Thank you for your letter of October 15, 1987 requesting a complete
summary of all federal government funding to forest and/or mining ventures
outside Canada from September 1984 to September 1987.
I am enclosing a list of Export Development Corporation, CIDA and PEMD
financial projects. I hope you find this information helpful.
I am sure Hon. Members will find it helpful, because I think many know what was supposed to occur within Canada. I see that the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) is here. He was one of the great promoters of a full Ministry of Forests in Canada. Forestry is our largest industry. More than one million Canadians are directly or indirectly employed in the forest sector. I think it is worth taking a look at what kind of assistance the Government is providing outside Canada that it refuses to provide inside Canada.
Let me deal first with the funding provided for mining. Funding is going to Chile, to the Chuquicamata copper mine. A very substantial amount of money is going there. Funds are

going to New Guinea, again to Chile and to Brazil. Under the CIDA projects, there is funding going to Botswana for mining, Botswana for training of diamond drillers, Ivory Coast and Ghana for gold mining.
There has been a fair amount of coverage in Canada and in North America generally about the problems that are being found in Brazil through this particular kind of funding, funding provided for small-scale gold exploration and for the training in mineral exploration by the Government of Canada to Brazil. There has been rather notorious coverage given to the fact that there is wholesale slaughter and murder of the indigenous populations in Brazil in the midst of the gold rush in that country. In fact, experts on the impact of these kinds of projects on the forests and on the indigenous people were here in Ottawa just a few weeks ago, pointing out how terrible the impact is on the indigenous and aboriginal populations in South America of some of the kinds of so-called booms that are going on. It is extremely short-sighted of Canada to be involved in funding projects which are part of the murderous slaughter of aboriginal people in South America.
Many Canadians would also be interested to know that the Government of Canada is funding a geochemical survey and various forms of technical assistance in Jamaica on the impoundment of bauxite tailings and metallic mineral surveys. Many, if not most, Canadians know that Alcan and others are the principal beneficiaries of bauxite mining in Jamaica. The Government of Canada, through so-called foreign aid, is doing what Alcan and others would like to see done in terms of such developments.
With regard to the problems which Third World countries are having in meeting their loan payments, as I said, Third World countries paid the IMF $5.9 billion more than they received last year with commercial banks taking more than they loaned. Let us look at the kinds of projects Canada has been funding in some of these countries.
In the Asian region, on forest projects alone, Canada has supplied $98,766 million in funding, a very substantial amount of money. Some of the funded projects are good and I think all Canadians would support them. For example, $46,250 million was spent in India on social forestry.
The harvesting of wood and the over-consumption of plants by various ungulates, whether goats, cattle, or whatever, has created a serious problem of desertification in many areas of the world. I am sure all Canadians support programs which lead toward soil conservation, the redevelopment of forest bases, and all that comes with them in terms of genetic diversity and so on.
Many Canadians scratch their heads when they realize the level of funding being provided by the Government for programs for the training of forest industry workers outside of Canada, which programs are also needed in Canada but are not available here. Let me give some examples of that. In
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
Indonesia we fund a forest industry vocational school as well as programs in fire management, forest management, and rural development and forestry. As I said the funding for that amounts to over $98 million at the present time. In Anglo Africa, Canada is providing $19.4 million for forest equipment credit, agriforestry nursery and extension in the Sudan, and institutional buildings and training in Rwanda.
In Francophone Africa the region total is $139.45 million. In the Cameroun, for example, we provide a forest equipment credit of $12 million. In Zaire we fund charcoal production technology as well as professional forestry training at $3.2 million. Institutional buildings are being constructed in Niger at a cost of $12.1 million.
It is quite proper that we are providing this program funding to Third World countries which require this assistance, but it is amazing that in our country our largest industry does not have a national Minister of Forests. In fact, the Minister of Forests has been delegated responsibilities for mining, and the Canadian Forest Service has been much downgraded since the Government took office.
Funding in the Americas and the Caribbean total $68,365 million. An example which drew my attention is the funding going to St. Lucia, an area about one-tenth the size of South Moresby. This year, $5.5 million is being provided for management and conservation of forests there. That is an interesting expenditure when various regions of British Columbia have been asking for program funds for postsecondary institutional training for forest workers and cannot get it. We have been looking for funding for dealing more extensively with what is known as the not satisfactorily restocked backlog and cannot get additional funding for that.
Nine of the ten federal-provincial agreements are coming up for renegotiation. It appears that the Government is not planning to carry on that A-base funding for five-year commitments to reforestation in Canada but seems to be able to find hundreds of millions for outside of Canada.
In Honduras $12.3 million is being provided this year for tropical forest development and management. In Peru $3.85 million is being provided for forestry university buildings. Peru is being given an equipment line of credit of $26 million and $6.1 million for forestry technical schools.
It is interesting that the Government provides funding to institutions outside of Canada for post-doctoral studies in forestry and does not provide it to a single university or college in Canada. It is a very interesting concept that many kinds of post-secondary educational development is fully funded by Canada outside our country but is not provided to Canadians unless they want to leave Canada.
I think Canadians would be interested in hearing about EDC financing. Let us keep in mind that the Secretary of State for External Affairs and others in the Government of Canada cite $2.7 billion as financing for foreign aid programs in Third World countries.

As an example, $19 million is going to Compania de Carbones of Chile for the construction of an open-pit mine and a bulk loading marine coal terminal. In addition, they are getting $874,000 for coal handling and ship loading, $79,000 for six 120-D and seven 35-D rear dump trucks. Millions of dollars are being spent on electrostatic precipitators, hydraulic rock breakers, mobile rock breakers, coal mining equipment, traction thickeners, flotation mechanisms, and two sag mills with liners. The list goes on and on. Seventy-six million dollars is being spent on mining equipment for the BAO coal project in China.
We must keep in mind that this funding is called foreign aid. Which Canadian companies are getting the foreign aid? Spar Aerospace is getting $765,000 to put in satellite ground station equipment in China. De Havilland is getting $1.6 million for Twin Otter aircraft and spares to go to China. Euclid is getting foreign aid which is going to the United Mizrahi Bank in Israel to acquire seven 100 ton rear-haul dump trucks. The Bank Hapoalim, again in Israel, is getting funding for wire screening line. The lists go on and on. Millions and millions of dollars are going to all kinds of Canadian companies to assist the borrower to buy equipment which will quite often, particularly in the mining sector, go into direct competition with Canadian operations.
Another example is Timberjack which is getting funding to provide seven Model-380 Timberjack log skidders to Chile. That is interesting in light of the human rights allegations our own Secretary of State of State for External Affairs has made against Chile.
I will conclude with just one more example. I know that the Minister of Science and Technology is interested in this because he used very similar information in boondoggling the Liberals in British Columbia prior to the last election. I will just remind the Minister that $900 million of the record profits two years in a row of MacMillan Bloedel is going to Tasmania to open a pulp mill.
The Government is putting no new money into reforestation, silviculture, post-secondary education or anything else in British Columbia. Where are the great promises of the Government to provide at least the the kinds of programs and assistance to post-secondary education within Canada which it provides so glowingly to countries outside of Canada?

Madam Speaker, we are discussing an Act to amend the Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act. The contribution I would like to make to the debate concerns the effect the arms race has on economic policies and conditions in both developed and underdeveloped countries. It is important to point out, particularly to Canadians who feel they do not contribute very much to the arms race, that that is not true. We are almost like prisoners of war because of the arms race. Our standard of living has been reduced because of the arms race.
The world spends well over $1 trillion a year on arms. It is estimated that in the U.S. over $500 million a day is spent on arms production. You cannot take $1 trillion out of the world's economy without reducing everyone's standard of living. Let me illustrate how we in Canada pay for the arms race and because we do we are economic prisoners of war.
Normally interest rates are generally one or two points above inflation. We now have an inflation rate of approximately 4 per cent and interest rates should be around 6 per cent. Indeed, a 6 per cent interest rate on mortgages, government debt, and farm debt, would alleviate much of the hardship that working men and women, including farmers, in Canada experience. Certainly a 6 per cent interest rate would make mortgages much less expensive. Today, families often require two income earners in order to provide the basic necessity of a roof over one's head, when only one income earner was needed in previous generations.
Why are interest rates so high? I maintain that it is because of the arms race. The deficit in the United States is so large that interest on that deficit requires 90 per cent of total U.S. savings, including individuals, corporations and businesses, just to service that debt. The United States must have a strong American dollar to provide for its capital needs and therefore must have high interest rates to attract international capital. Of course, Canada's interest rate is directly tied to the American interest rate. We also need a higher interest rate to

May 27, 1988
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
maintain capital at home and attract capital from abroad. For that reason, our interest rate is substantially more than the 2 per cent or 3 per cent over the inflation rate. That is the way in which Canadians pay for the arms race. If it was not for the arms race, our mortgage payments would be less, debt payments for farmers would be less, and the debt payments of the Government would be less. It is estimated that for every one percentage drop in interest rates the public treasury in Canada saves $1 billion. The arms race affects us all because it costs money and reduces our standard of living.
We live in an age of unprecedented abundance, with a technological ability to produce that is unparalleled in the history of the human race. Yet we live in an age of scarcity, when there is not enough money to provide decent housing, medical attention, educational facilities, and old age facilities for our society. We cannot afford to provide decent health care or decent housing for our old and our infirm. We cannot look after our mentally disabled because the Government says it does not have the resources in an age of cut-backs and restrictions. The poor and disabled of society are the ones who suffer the most. Why do we live in an age of scarcity when we should be enjoying the benefits of abundance? Again, it is because of the arms race. The arms race sucks wealth from every country and channels it into the most useless form of production-arms production-at the expense of our farmers, home owners, our sick, young and disabled.
One hopeful result of the stock market crash last year is that perhaps the superpowers began to realize the economic limits to the arms race. That crash occurred because the arms race caused the United States to become the greatest debtor nation in the world. It could no longer continue to borrow money without international lenders realizing there was a limit.
The crisis of that stock market crash has not been resolved and the world economy stands on the brink of a major recession, if not a depression. It is more than a question of confidence, it is a question of how much longer the superpowers can continue spending so much money on arms production.
I believe they have reached the limit. Certainly the Soviet Union has realized it has reached that limit. The Soviet Union spends about as much on arms production as the United States but has half the gross domestic product. It can even less afford the arms build-up.
I suggest that if we are really interested in arms reduction and disarmament agreements, rather than send generals and diplomats to the negotiations, we should send officials from the Department of Finance and Treasury Board to determine how to reduce arms expenditures. I think people from the Finance Department and Treasury Board could find ways to reduce the arms expenditures that generals and diplomats have difficulty determining.
The Government has taken another step in human folly and stupidity with its venture into the big league by ordering nuclear submarines. When the world is beginning to realize the economic limits to the arms race, the Government believes it
can afford $11 billion or $12 billion for nuclear submarines to patrol our Arctic. That is insanity.
I appreciate this opportunity to link the arms race to the problems not only in Third World countries but in western industrialized countries as well. I appreciate this opportunity to talk about the cut-backs and restrictions that are taking place during this age of abundance. I realize the road to disarmament will be long and rough. Yet perhaps it is economic necessity that will force us down that road and I believe that once we take that step there will be some very hopeful signs for the human race.
We have the potential to produce enough for every man, woman and child so that we can provide clean water, decent health facilities and decent housing. We have the potential to overcome pestilence, disease and hunger. We only need to redirect that wealth away from the death machine and its production of armaments into what I call the human machine, the human race stands on the brink of a marvellous future.
I sincerely hope that this Parliament and Canada will play its part in helping humankind find a new and better direction.

Madam Speaker, I totally agree with my colleague. It is insane. The rest of the world, hopefully, is moving in the direction of disarmament, of lessening the arms race, in large part forced by economic necessity. The deficit in the United States is so high it just cannot continue with the arms build-up. It is, as are the Russians, being forced to sit down and begin negotiations to cut back. University programs are being cut back because there is not enough money for them. And we are spending billions of dollars for nuclear submarines. It is obscene. Of course, we cannot afford it. Of

Madam Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague from Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and my colleague from Regina East (Mr. de Jong) for their good acting talents. We should consider some facts that the Hon. Member for Regina East did not mention; for example, our Government cancelled Third World debt at the Francophone Summit. We finally had a Francophone Summit. We managed to make peace between France and Canada on our role in the French-speaking world and at this second Summit held in Quebec City, we reached an agreement to cancel Third World debt. This is something much more practical and it does much more to ease poverty in the Third World; it also gives an example to the world community of something practical to do, rather than make passionate speeches in the abstract, quite comfortably in this beautiful Chamber. Problems are solved out in the field.
So I find it most unfortunate that on such a major issue of practical importance, Hon. Members choose to play petty politics where the needs are so great.
They talk about poverty as if it were a soap opera. They talk about aid for the Third World; they talk about nuclear submarines as if it were a Rambo movie. It is really regrettable that for the past few minutes, they have lowered the level of this debate on such an important issue by petty politicking. So I would ask my colleague from Regina East (Mr. de Jong) why he forgot to mention in his presentation that we, the Progressive Conservative Government of Canada, took the first step to cancelling the Third World debt. We converted the loans to grants and that is what the Third World was asking us to do, because we believe that we should give people what they want and not what we want to give them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tomorrow is May 28, the day that marks the seventieth anniversary of the establishment of the Republic of Armenia. This will be a day of celebration for a nation whose resilience and cohesiveness endure in spite of the tragedies which it has encountered.
I thank Hon. Members of the House in all Parties who attended a meeting yesterday with members of the Armenian community of Canada. It was the best attended meeting we have ever had over the years. where in a Canada that is growing and developing, we can show the rest of the world what all of us together, belonging to different races, groups and nationalities, are able to do.

Mr. Speaker, next week is National Environment Week, a chance for Canadians to reaffirm their commitment to "our common future", a chance to explore our natural heritage and work together to conserve and protect the environment.
In Parkdale-High Park, National Environment Week provides a focus for concerns over the water quality of Lake Ontario and the Humber River, pollution of the Western Beaches, and environmental safety in the Junction Triangle, while underscoring our commitment to a comprehensive cleanup.
Across Canada hundreds of activities are planned from St. John's, Newfoundland, to Dawson City, Yukon. Canadians will plant trees, clean up litter, attend films and lectures, meet fellow environmentalists, and take the time to enjoy nature- by bicycle, boat, or on foot.
National Environment Week provides a chance for everyone to take an active role. It is up to all of us-federal, provincial, municipal Governments, and concerned citizens-to work together to preserve and conserve our environment.

CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-CONTENT OF IMPLEMENTING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just when it was safe for Canadians to go to bed again, just when we were beginning to feel safe about walking the streets again, it happened. Canadians were just beginning to relax, content in the security of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) promise that our country would not be sold out to the Americans, that we would not become the fifty-first State. Then it happened. The legislation was tabled.
I was going to send a copy of the legislation to some of my constituents who are particularly interested in this matter. Thus I was browsing through it the other night to make sure that there was nothing that would disturb them unduly. And then I saw it, page 99: "every reference in those provisions to Canadian shall be read and construed as a reference to American." I could not believe it so I read on: "every reference to-Canadian-controlled shall be read-as	Americancontrolled." The Prime Minister's promise began to dim.
It went on: "the reference to Canada shall be read and construed as a reference to the United States." The real purpose of the trade deal began to crystallize.


May 27, 1988

Then, finally: "Where two persons, one being a Canadian and the other being an American, own equally all of the voting shares of a corporation, the corporation is deemed to be American-controlled."
I finally understood what the Americans had accomplished with this trade deal. It is summed up in the old adage: What's yours is mine, and what's mine is my own.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the federal Government will be spending an additional half a billion dollars over the next five years to nurture and enhance research and development in Canadian universities.
The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret) and the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) announced Wednesday a $240 million program to establish Centres of Excellence, and a $200 million increase in the base budgets of the university research granting councils.
The Centres of Excellence will encourage a partnership between the universities, industry, and government, a partnership in world-class research and Canadian competitiveness, a partnership in progress.
New federal funding for the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, the Medical Research Council, and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council is welcome support for research and training in Canadian universities.
These two new federal government initiatives are good for the universities, and good for Canada, for it is in our Canadian universities where new ideas are developed and where the skills of young Canadians are honed.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great relief to see that Soviet soldiers have finally started to leave Afghanistan. For too long, the Soviet Union tried to support the Communist regime in Kabul.
As in the case of U.S. intervention in South East Asia during the sixties and seventies, the Soviets became involved in a brutal, senseless war.
After tens of thousands of Soviet soldiers were wounded or killed, it finally became clear the situation could not go on.
A captain in the Soviet army recently wondered why this had to happen. The question may never be answered, not in Vietnam and not in Afghanistan.
Secretary General Gorbachev is to be commended for his decision to withdraw from Afghanistan, and we hope the Soviet authorities have learned a lesson from this unfortunate experience.
Yesterday Vietnam, today Afghanistan. Let us hope the superpowers will understand they should influence the peoples of this world through their outstanding achievements in science, medicine and the arts, not with bayonets.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-EFFECT ON WESTERN CANADA
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-EFFECT ON WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most analysts agree that the free trade agreement will benefit western Canada. For the past four years the Canada West Foundation, a non-profit western based research institute, has done extensive research on the free trade issue. Its study confirms what others have said, that is, the free trade agreement is good for western Canada.
The study indicates that 15.3 per cent of the labour force will benefit directly from the free trade agreement. However, the importance of this is shown by the fact that these sectors represent 25 per cent of the combined output of the Gross Domestic Product of the four western provinces. Only 1 per cent of the sectors are negatively affected.
The biggest winners will be agriculture and energy. Livestock producers in western Canada are regarded as the clear winners. In energy, oil, gas, and electricity, producers support the enhanced access to and secure market of the U.S. Easing National Energy Board export regulations under the free trade agreement is a positive development for the western Canadian economy.
In my own province of Saskatchewan sectors directly benefiting from the free trade agreement account for 20 per cent of the provincial Gross Domestic Product, and only 1 per cent of the industries will be adversely affected.
I urge people of western Canada to get a copy of this report and read it. It is very informative, and I think it spells out the major advantages of what the free trade agreement will accomplish for us in the West.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-IMPACT ON BRITISH COLUMBIA
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-IMPACT ON BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in British Columbia often like to ask the federal Government: "What have you done for us lately?" I am proud to reply: "The Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement".
This has recently been confirmed by the prestigious Canada West Foundation's report on the impact of the free trade agreement on the West. In that report, the Foundation found that in British Columbia the sectors directly benefiting from the free trade agreement account for 18 per cent of the province's gross domestic product, while those which might be adversely affected account for only 2.4 per cent.
In that report it is also pointed out that secure access to U.S. markets should facilitate investment, production, and job growth in forestry products, natural gas, minerals, precious metals, and in other sectors.
While all regions of the province will benefit, Vancouver can particularly expect to gain as a result of its proximity to the large U.S. Pacific markets and its excellent range of transportation services for exporters.
I have not even talked about the potential new capital investment that will be attracted from the Pacific Rim. What it all adds up to is that this free trade agreement creates the prospects for British Columbia to fulfil, not only its natural resource potential, but the resource of its people.
What is my advice? Go West, young men and women.
May 27, 1988

subtopic: DROUGHT IN SOUTHERN PRAIRIES-NEED FOR GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
DROUGHT IN SOUTHERN PRAIRIES-NEED FOR GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been another dry week on most of the southern prairies. According to a PFRA water supply update, conditions are so severe that the South Saskatchewan River at Medicine Hat, Alberta, is flowing at a rate of 31 cubic metres a second. Historically it moves at a minimum of 133 cubic feet a second and up to 435 cubic feet per second.
Shallow wells are going dry in southwest Saskatchewan and southeast Alberta. On-farm water supplies are low. Shallow wells generally provide the best drinking water; towns and villages are watching these sources disappear.
The situation is particularly crucial for ranchers who are having to truck water and feed to livestock. Cattlemen in the British Columbia interior are also affected.
The area was hit by a drought in 1981, 1984, 1985, and again this year. After the 1985 drought the federal Government gave $150 million to producers of grain and forage, plus $48 million to livestock producers. Given the odds, Canada will have to find at least another $200 million this year to provide assistance with water and feed.

Mr. Speaker, on occasion an Hon. Member will stand in the House and extol the virtues of one or more of his or her constituents. Since the Northlands Coliseum is in my riding of Edmonton East, I would like to say a word about 20 of my own constituents who work at Northlands. Of course I am referring to the Edmonton Oilers, who last night captured their second consecutive Stanley Cup, and what a feat!
I could go on and on about Sather, Gretzky, Messier, Fuhr, and the rest of the boys. Instead, I would like to say a few words about Edmonton, the City of Champions.
I suppose that Edmontonians can no longer claim that we are not getting our "fair share". Along with the Oilers' four Stanley Cups in the past five years, the Edmonton Eskimos have long been a CFL powerhouse, and their 1987 Grey Cup win over Toronto proved that Canadian football is as exciting and viable as any sport anywhere.
Let us not forget Edmonton's Pat Ryan, whose rink last year captured the Canadian Brier, Canada's National Men's Curling Championship.
I trust that Canadians will not begrudge Edmonton for commandeering so many of our treasured national sports titles.
I hope that they recognize the Alberta capital for what it consistently is-the City of Champions!

subtopic: OPPOSITION TO PURCHASE OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
OPPOSITION TO PURCHASE OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, more than two-thirds of Canadians are opposed to the Mulroney plan to purchase nuclear submarines for Canada. The price tag will run to at least $16 billion and Canadians oppose both the purposes and the price.
On Wednesday of this week we learned of the fact that on at least 63 occasions warships and submarines carrying nuclear weapons visited Canada. Federal government records show 18 such visits at Halifax during 1987, 11 visits at Nanoose on Vancouver Island, 10 visits at Vancouver, and 24 at Esquimalt.
The United States is violating Canada's sovereignty in our ports, and it is violating the spirit of Canada's position of not having nuclear weapons on our territory, by bringing nuclear weapons into the downtown areas of some of our major cities.
The nuclear arms race at sea is accelerating. By the end of 1987, 1,101 ships and submarines, and more than 3,250 aircraft could fire, transport, or service nuclear weapons.
Do Canadians want to join in the race to Armageddon or to peace? Two-thirds of Canadians think that the purchase of nuclear submarines is wrong. Canada's Arctic, and all of the Arctic, must become demilitarized and denuclearized.
Our tax dollars would be better spent on a peace institute and serious moves to disengage constructively from warlike activity and development.

Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Grains and
Oilseeds)): Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member raises an important issue. It is a favourite ploy of the Europeans to talk about numbers and use percentages. People should be aware of the facts and I will just give three examples to the Hon. Member.
A Canadian wheat farmer now receives about $2.91 a bushel. The European farmer receives $7.13 a bushel.
A Canadian farmer receives about $1.10 for a bushel of Canadian Wheat Board barley, although the off-board market is up a little bit. The European producer receives $5.42 a bushel.
Canadian farmers receive almost $7 a bushel for soy-beans, but in Europe it is about three times that amount.
We should look at the real numbers and compare what a European farmer gets as opposed to what a Canadian farmer gets, and get away from percentages and the kind of games the Europeans like to play. If we do that, we realize that the Europeans are being subsidized substantially more than Canadians.

The House resumed from Thursday, May 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-129, an Act to provide for the continuance of Air Canada under the Canada Business Corporations Act and for the issuance and sale of shares thereof to the public, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to join in this debate for a number of reasons. First, the constituency of Brampton-Georgetown is adjacent to Toronto International Airport. Therefore there are a great many employees from Air Canada who live in my constituency. Over the years these employees have made representations to me, as have various committees that have been formed by the staff and the unions, to discuss the issue of the privatization of Air Canada. Members of the union leadership have been into my office to discuss the privatization of Air Canada. They have expressed concern with respect to it. However, many of the workers who have come in to see me or who have met me on the street in my riding have informed me that in no uncertain terms they are very pleased with the actions of the Government in proceeding with the privatization of Air Canada under Bill C-129 which we are debating today.
I must say that I am very pleased at the action that the Government has taken as well. I think most Members in the House would agree that as Members of Parliament we do a fair amount of travelling and that we have the opportunity to travel on many airlines throughout the world. In my capacity as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and now in my capacity as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade I have had the pleasure of representing Canada around the world. I consider it a privilege to be able to travel on many airlines.


May 27, 1988

I am a great comparison shopper. I am pleased and proud to say that Air Canada competes with the finest airlines in the world. There is no question about it. The quality of service, the staff, the attitude and the leadership in aviation shown by Air Canada are all unquestioned. Thus I am standing with a great deal of confidence in knowing that the management of Air Canada is perfectly capable of competing in the world, in the private sector, in the air transportation business. I believe that management is extremely pleased with this decision as well.
At one time Air Canada served a public policy purpose in Canada. I believe that Canada is one of the toughest countries in the world to govern because of the vast distances between centres of population and because of its vast size. Thus transportation is very important. As the airline industry grew, various airlines in this country grew and matured. At the beginning we had to ensure that good, safe, and competent services were provided for all areas and regions of the country. In the beginning, and for a number of years, Air Canada was the tool that we used to achieve that.
Today the industry has matured tremendously. We as Canadians can be very proud of the various airlines that we have, and Air Canada is one of those. It is time that Air Canada competed on an equal basis with the other airlines in Canada that have developed and matured over the years. Because of the maturity of the organization, the public policy purpose for Air Canada no longer exists. Needless to say, I am very pleased to participate in this debate and support the Bill wholeheartedly.
There is not only great support from the staff of Air Canada, but generally I believe the public is supporting this move. Simply stated, the privatization program of the Government of Canada is if it does not serve a public policy purpose, then it should not be in government hands.
The success stories of those companies that have been privatized are nothing short of spectacular. De Havilland is one such example. For the period of time we debated in the House the privatization of de Havilland, we heard the Liberal Member who represents that area say how disastrous that it was going to be. He stood out in front of the plant and handed out pamphlets that stated that this was the demise of the company, it was going to be terrible, and what a terrible fate was ahead for the group of workers at de Havilland.
As it turned out, I believe there are 1,200 to 1,500 more employees at that plant. The plant has been modernized and streamlined. A few day ago I met with the president and he was excited and enthusiastic about what is going on. They are designing a much larger Dash-8, their sales are tremendous, and the prospects for the future are great. One can look at some 14 other privatizations that have taken place. They are all success stories. I have no doubt whatsoever that Air Canada will also be a success story.
Air Canada
We want to get this debate into committee in order that the committee can examine how the privatization will be carried out, hear representations from the public on their thoughts. Because this is such an important item and because the Government places such a priority on it, and because the Opposition is not very enthusiastic in its opposition, if the truth were known, I think that the Opposition would support this wholeheartedly, especially my friends in the New Democratic Party. If they talked to those ordinary Canadians whom they are always preaching about over there, if they talked to the people who handle the baggage, who take the reservations, the air crew, pilots, and so on, they would find out that the staff is very much in favour of this and looking forward to actively participating in the operation and the share ownership of that company. Because it is so wanted throughout the country, not only by staff but also by the general public, I move:
That the question be now put.
Agreed.
